{{Wikispecies|Samolus valerandi}}
'''''Samolus valerandi''''' is a [[species]] of [[Semiaquatic|semi-aquatic]] [[flowering plant]] in the primrose [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Primulaceae]]. Common names include '''seaside brookweed''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SAVA3|taxon=Samolus valerandi|accessdate=28 October 2015}}</ref> '''brookweed''',<ref name=Weakley>{{cite web |url= http://www.herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm |title= Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States |author= Alan Weakley |date= 2015 |access-date= 2018-02-06 |archive-date= 2018-10-06 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181006082209/http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm }}</ref> '''thin-leaf brookweed''', '''water cabbage''' and '''water rose'''.<ref>Huxley. A. ''The New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. 1992. MacMillan Press 1992 {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}</ref>

==Description==
It is a small perennial, growing to around 35 cm (13.8 inches) high. Its inflorescence is a raceme, with small white flowers on long stalks. Its corollas have five lobes. It can produce flowers throughout the growing season, from spring to fall. Its fruits are capsules that are green and globose.<ref name=Missouri>{{cite book |last=Yatskievych |first=George |date=2013 |title=Flora of Missouri, Volume 3 |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press |page=793 }}</ref> 
<gallery widths="200px" heights="200px">
Image:Samolus parviflorus.jpg|Mature inflorescences are widely spreading, with fruits on long stalks.
</gallery>

==Taxonomy==
Although some floras recognize the North American populations of ''S. valerandi'' as a separate species (''S. parviflorus'') or subspecies (''S. valerandi'' ssp. ''parviflorus''),<ref name=fna>{{cite web |title=Samolus |work=Flora of North America |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417215 |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=2018-02-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Samolus parviflorus |url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-taxon=Samolus+parviflorus |website=www.calflora.org |publisher=Calflora |access-date=1 February 2018}}</ref> a 2012 investigation based on molecular and morphological data indicated that ''S. vagans'' and ''S. parviflorus'' should not be regarded as separate species but as part of a widespread "''S. valerandi'' species complex".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=K. |last2=Anderberg |first2=A. A. |last3=Ronse De Craene |first3=L. P. |last4=Wanntorp |first4=L. |title=Origin, diversification, and evolution of Samolus valerandi (Samolaceae, Ericales) |journal=[[Plant Systematics and Evolution]] |date=23 June 2012 |volume=298 |issue=8 |pages=1523–1531 |doi=10.1007/s00606-012-0655-z|s2cid=15115821 }}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Samolus valerandi'' is widely distributed across western and Mediterranean [[Europe]], north [[Africa]], [[Asia]] and [[Australia]], [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]] including Cuba, and Japan.<ref name=dvf>{{cite web |title=Den Virtuella Floran |vauthors=Anderberg A,Anderberg AL |publisher=Swedish Museum of Natural History (Naturhistorika Riksmuseet) |date=2017|url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/primula/samola/samovalv.jpg |access-date=9 July 2021}}</ref>

==Ecological aspects==
This species is found in a variety of wet habitats, including stream banks, tidal marshes, and seeps.<ref name=Weakley/> It can be found in both degraded and intact natural communities.<ref>[http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/brookweed.htm IllinoisWildflowers]</ref>

==Cultivation==
The plant can be grown in [[pond]]s, bog gardens, and damp areas in the garden. ''S. valerandi'' prefers light (sandy), medium (loamy), and heavy (clay) soils, preferably neutral or basic (alkaline) soils. It can tolerate both shade and a bright, sunny position. It requires moist or wet soil and can even grow in water. The plant can tolerate maritime exposure and is self-fertile. ''S. valerandi'' is sometimes grown in [[aquarium]]s, although they seem to last only a limited time when grown fully submersed.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

===Uses===
The plant's leaves, when cut and agitated in water, produce a lather, for which reason in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]] it has been used by the local Arab population, in former times, to launder clothes and was called by them ''sabūn 'arab'' (= Arab soap).<ref>{{cite book|last=Ḳrispil|first=Nissim|title=A Bag of Plants (The Useful Plants of Israel) (Yalḳuṭ ha-tsemaḥim)|editor=Amos Shapira |publisher=Ya'arah Publishing House Ltd.|volume=4 (N.-Ṣ.) |year=1987|location=Jerusalem|pages=990–993|language=he|oclc=21934597}}, s.v. Samolus valerandi</ref>
